claim: The bacterial flagellar filament is several times longer than a bacterial cell body and is made out of up to 20,000 flagellin subunits.
source: The external flagellar filament is several times longer than a bacterial cell body and is made out of up to 20,000 flagellin subunits (Berg and Anderson, 1973; Chevance and Hughes, 2008; Macnab, 2003; Silverman and Simon, 1974) (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations and reference to Figure 1a

claim: A type III export apparatus located at the base of the flagellum utilizes the proton motive force (pmf) as the primary energy source to translocate axial components of the flagellum across the inner membrane.
source: A type III export apparatus located at the base of the flagellum utilizes the proton motive force (pmf) as the primary energy source to translocate axial components of the flagellum across the inner membrane (Minamino and Namba, 2008; Paul et al., 2008; Minamino et al., 2011; Erhardt et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple literature citations

claim: Exported substrates travel through a narrow 2 nm channel within the structure and self-assemble at the tip of the growing flagellum.
source: Exported substrates travel through a narrow 2 nm channel within the structure and self-assemble at the tip of the growing flagellum.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge about flagellar assembly

claim: An exponential decay of filament elongation with length was observed using electron microscopic measurements, which was proposed to be a result of decreased translocation efficiency.
source: An exponential decay of filament elongation with length was observed using electron microscopic measurements, which was proposed to be a result of decreased translocation efficiency (Iino, 1974; Tanner et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: A recent study used dual-colour fluorescent labelling of flagellar filaments to distinguish basal from apical filament growth and found that the rate of polymerization was independent of filament length.
source: A recent study used dual-colour fluorescent labelling of flagellar filaments to distinguish basal from apical filament growth and found that the rate of polymerization was independent of filament length (Turner et al., 2012; Stern and Berg, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: A model based on the pulling force of a filament-spanning chain of flagellin subunits was proposed to explain the apparent length-independent growth.
source: A model based on the pulling force of a filament-spanning chain of flagellin subunits was proposed to explain the apparent length-independent growth (Evans et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: The amount of extracellular flagellin was approximately 1.6-fold higher in the ΔflgK mutant compared to wild-type cells.
source: The amount of extracellular flagellin was approximately 1.6-fold higher in the ΔflgK mutant compared to wild-type cells.
evidence: Experimental observation from the study, supported by data in Figure 1b

claim: Cytoplasmic flagellin was substantially more abundant in the wild-type than in the ΔflgK mutant.
source: Consistently, cytoplasmic flagellin was substantially more abundant in the wild-type than in the ΔflgK mutant (Figure 1b).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by Figure 1b

claim: Only a small fraction of the total flagellin is leaked in monomeric form by wild-type cells during filament formation.
source: Measurements of flagellin leakage during filament formation revealed that only a small fraction of the total flagellin is leaked in monomeric form by wild-type cells during filament formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Experimental observation supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The majority of exported flagellin subunits are incorporated into the growing filament under the experimental conditions.
source: demonstrating that the majority of exported flagellin subunits are incorporated into the growing filament under our experimental conditions.
evidence: Inference from the flagellin leakage measurements

claim: The presence of an assembled filament decreases the rate of flagellin transport.
source: These results indicate that the presence of an assembled filament decreases the rate of flagellin transport, which is consistent with the decreased rates of FlgE and FliK export in a long hook mutant (Koroyasu et al., 1998; Erhardt et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference from experimental results, supported by citations to previous studies

claim: A similar filament length-dependent effect on flagellin transport was observed in a mutant of the flagellin-specific cytoplasmic chaperone FliS.
source: A similar filament length-dependent effect on flagellin transport was also observed in a mutant of the flagellin-specific cytoplasmic chaperone FliS (Figure 1b).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by Figure 1b

claim: FliS promotes docking and subsequent unfolding of flagellin at the export apparatus.
source: FliS promotes docking and subsequent unfolding of flagellin at the export apparatus (Kinoshita et al., 2013; Furukawa et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The flagellin injection rate at the export apparatus substantially contributes to the flagellum growth dynamics.
source: suggesting that the flagellin injection rate at the export apparatus substantially contributes to the flagellum growth dynamics.
evidence: Inference from the experimental observations with FliS mutant

claim: The initial filament growth rate was ~83 nm∙min−1, which decreased over time.
source: The initial filament growth rate was ~83 nm∙min−1, which decreased over time (Figure 1e).
evidence: Experimental measurement from population-based immunostaining, supported by Figure 1e

claim: An initial filament growth rate of ~100 nm∙min−1 was observed using continuous in situ immunostaining, which decreased over time.
source: We observed an initial filament growth rate of ~100 nm∙min−1, which decreased over time similar as for the population-wide approach described above (Figure 1f, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Experimental measurement from real-time imaging, supported by Figure 1f

claim: Turner et al. (2012) measured the growth kinetics of individual filaments in Escherichia coli and reported a length independent growth rate of ~13 nm∙min−1.
source: In a previous study, Turner et al. (2012) measured the growth kinetics of individual filaments in Escherichia coli by site-specific labelling of flagellin subunits containing an exposed cysteine residue using sulfhydryl-specific (maleimide) fluorochromes and reported a length independent growth rate of ~13 nm∙min−1.
evidence: Citation to previous study

claim: Triple labelling demonstrated that the extension length of the filament (apical fragment) is inversely proportional to its initial length (basal fragment), until the growth rate for long filaments decreases to a point where it becomes minimal.
source: Triple labelling (exchange of dyes three times) demonstrated that the extension length of the filament (apical fragment) is inversely proportional to its initial length (basal fragment), until the growth rate for long filaments decreases to a point where it becomes minimal (Figure 2).
evidence: Experimental observation from triple labelling experiments, supported by Figure 2

claim: Multiple labelling of flagellar filaments confirmed the length-dependent elongation mechanism with an elongation speed decreasing gradually from ~100 nm∙min−1 to ~20 nm∙min−1.
source: The multiple labelling of flagellar filaments confirmed the length-dependent elongation mechanism with an elongation speed decreasing gradually from ~100 nm∙min−1 to ~20 nm∙min−1 (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental observation from multiple labelling experiments, supported by Figure 3

claim: Only a minor fraction of flagella broke or stopped growing during the experiment.
source: We note that we only observed a minor fraction of flagella that broke or stopped growing during the experiment (Figure 3e).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by Figure 3e

claim: Flagellin monomers, which are at least partially α-helical inside the channel, are pushed by a pmf-driven export apparatus into the channel and move diffusively in one dimension through the length of the flagellum.
source: Derivation of this formula is based on an injection-diffusion model where flagellin monomers, which are at least partially α-helical inside the channel (Shibata et al., 2007), are pushed by a pmf-driven export apparatus into the channel and move diffusively in one dimension through the length of the flagellum (Stern and Berg, 2013; Keener, 2006).
evidence: Model description based on citations and previous knowledge

claim: The diffusion coefficient D is estimated to be approximately 5.25 × 10−13 m2 ⋅ s−1.
source: From all the datasets presented above, we determined a ≈ 0.2 µm2 ⋅ min−1. Using β = 0.47 nm (a flagellar filament of 1 µm length is composed of approximately 2130 flagellin subunits [Yonekura et al., 2003]), l = 74 nm (assuming an extended, α-helical flagellin molecule) this leads to an estimate of D ≈ 5.25 × 10−13 m2 ⋅ s−1.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data and known structural parameters

claim: Stern and Berg estimated D ≈ 5.78 × 10−11 m2 ⋅ s−1 for freely moving α-helical flagellin in water.
source: Stern and Berg (Stern and Berg, 2013) estimated D ≈ 5.78 × 10−11 m2 ⋅ s−1 for freely moving α-helical flagellin in water.
evidence: Citation to previous study

claim: The actual diffusion coefficient for movement in the narrow 2 nm channel would be substantially smaller than for freely moving flagellin in water.
source: The actual diffusion coefficient for movement in the narrow 2 nm channel would be substantially smaller, however.
evidence: Inference based on physical constraints

claim: Stern and Berg used a 480 times smaller diffusion coefficient (D ≈ 1.25 × 10−13 m2 ⋅ s−1) for numerical simulations that resulted in a declining growth curve.
source: Stern and Berg (Stern and Berg, 2013) (their Figure 2) used a 480 times smaller diffusion coefficient (D ≈ 1.25 × 10−13 m2 ⋅ s−1) for numerical simulations that resulted in a declining growth curve, which closely resembled the filament growth kinetics presented above.
evidence: Citation to previous study

claim: The growth of a new part of the filament (apical fragment) shows a strong inverse dependence on its initial length (basal fragment) for short filaments, while the growth rate for long filaments decreases to a point where this dependence becomes minimal.
source: Our triple and multiple labelling experiments demonstrated that the growth of a new part of the filament (apical fragment) shows a strong inverse dependence on its initial length (basal fragment) for short filaments, while the growth rate for long filaments decreases to a point where this dependence becomes minimal (Figure 2, Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental observation from triple and multiple labelling experiments

claim: Several differences in the experimental setup of Turner et al. (2012) from ours might have affected the injection rate and frequency of filament breakage.
source: We note that several differences in the experimental setup of Turner et al. (2012) from ours might have affected the injection rate and frequency of filament breakage.
evidence: Inference comparing experimental methods

claim: The possibility of broken/stalled filaments and possible perturbations of the injection rate reconcile our data with the reported filament growth data of Turner et al. (2012).
source: As described in detail in Appendix 1, the possibility of broken/stalled filaments and possible perturbations of the injection rate reconcile our data with the reported filament growth data of Turner et al. (2012) and explains why we observed a length-dependent decrease in growth rate.
evidence: Inference from simulations and analysis

claim: Simulated broken/stalled filaments accumulate on the x-axis, which results in a quasi-linear fit of the complete filament growth rate data, similar to the linear filament growth observed by Turner et al. (2012).
source: The simulated broken/stalled filaments accumulate on the x-axis, which results in a quasi-linear fit of the complete filament growth rate data, similar to the linear filament growth observed by Turner et al. (2012).
evidence: Simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: A length-dependent decrease in filament growth rate would explain why flagellar filaments do not grow indefinitely.
source: We further note that a length-dependent decrease in filament growth rate would explain why flagellar filaments do not growth indefinitely.
evidence: Inference from the model

claim: Flagellar filaments broken by mechanical shearing forces can re-grow.
source: However, flagellar filaments broken by mechanical shearing forces can re-grow (Turner et al., 2012; Rosu and Hughes, 2006; Vogler et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: The injection-diffusion model predicts that the elongation rate of re-growing filaments would increase compared to unbroken filaments.
source: The injection-diffusion model predicts that the elongation rate of re-growing filaments would increase compared to unbroken filaments.
evidence: Prediction from the mathematical model

claim: The elongation rate of re-growing, previously broken filaments was substantially faster than the elongation rate of unbroken filaments and was dependent on the length of the basal filament segment.
source: Consistent with the injection-diffusion mechanism, the elongation rate of re-growing, previously broken filaments was substantially faster than the elongation rate of unbroken filaments and was dependent on the length of the basal filament segment, which remained attached to the bacterial cell surface (Figure 4).
evidence: Experimental observation from mechanical shearing experiments, supported by Figure 4

claim: Evans et al. demonstrated that N-terminal regions of flagellar substrates (FlgD, FlgE, FlgG and FliK) can bind to the C-terminal cytoplasmic domain of FlhB.
source: Evans et al. demonstrated that N-terminal regions of flagellar substrates (FlgD, FlgE, FlgG and FliK) can bind to the C-terminal cytoplasmic domain of FlhB, which is a component of the pmf-driven transmembrane export gate complex.
evidence: Citation to previous study by Evans et al.

claim: Site-specific cysteine-cysteine crosslinking showed that the N- and C-terminal regions of hook (FlgE) and flagellin (FliC) can interact to form head-to-tail dimers.
source: Further, site-specific cysteine-cysteine crosslinking showed that the N- and C-terminal regions of hook (FlgE) and flagellin (FliC) can interact to form head-to-tail dimers.
evidence: Citation to previous experimental results

claim: The 2 nm wide filament channel is too narrow to accommodate the secretion of much more than one folded α-helix.
source: A flagellum-spanning chain requires interactions of the N- and C-terminal α-helical domains of flagellin, but the 2 nm wide filament channel (Yonekura et al., 2003) is too narrow to accommodate the secretion of much more than one folded α-helix (Figure 5a).
evidence: Based on structural knowledge and citation, supported by Figure 5a

claim: The N- and C-termini of successive flagellin molecules are anti-parallel and far apart in the polymerized filament structure (~17 Å on average).
source: The chain mechanism hypothesizes that folding of a flagellin subunit at the tip of the flagellum can pull a chain of succeeding subunits, but the N- and C-termini of successive flagellin molecules are anti-parallel and far apart in the polymerized filament structure (∼17 Å on average) (Yonekura et al., 2003; Samatey et al., 2001) (Figure 5b).
evidence: Based on structural knowledge from citations, supported by Figure 5b

claim: Flagellar substrates such as FlgM or excess hook-associated proteins (FlgK, FlgL, FliD) are constantly exported during flagellum growth.
source: Flagellar substrates such as FlgM or excess hook-associated proteins (FlgK, FlgL, FliD) are constantly exported during flagellum growth (Komoriya et al., 1999) and do not interact with flagellin (Furukawa et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: Premature termination of translation is occurring frequently (~1∙10−4 to ~5∙10−4 events per codon).
source: Also, premature termination of translation is occurring frequently (~1∙10−4 to ~5∙10−4 events per codon) (Sin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous study

claim: A high proportion of 5–20% newly synthesized flagellin might be truncated for the C-terminal domain needed for head-to-tail chain formation.
source: Thus, a high proportion of 5–20% newly synthesized flagellin might be truncated for the C-terminal domain needed for head-to-tail chain formation.
evidence: Inference from the premature termination frequency

claim: Secretion of as little as one non-chaining substrate every 10,000 full-length flagellin molecules would prevent filament elongation if a chain mechanism drives flagellum growth.
source: We estimate that secretion of as little as one non-chaining substrate every 10,000 full-length flagellin molecules would prevent filament elongation if a chain mechanism drives flagellum growth (Figure 5d–g).
evidence: Estimation from modeling, supported by Figure 5d-g

claim: Competitive secretion of the flagellin truncation mutants did not affect endogenous flagellin transport during filament formation.
source: Competitive secretion of the flagellin truncation mutants did not affect endogenous flagellin transport during filament formation (Figure 5c).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by Figure 5c

claim: No significant difference was observed in filament extension kinetics when chain-disrupting flagellin mutants were co-expressed.
source: Filament extension kinetics were determined using multiple labelling of individual flagellar filaments and, similarly, no significant difference was observed when chain-disrupting flagellin mutants were co-expressed (Figure 5e, Figure 5—figure supplement 3c).
evidence: Experimental observation supported by Figure 5e

claim: Mathematical modelling of the chain model-dependent filament elongation dynamics predicted a linear growth up to a very long flagellum (>0.1 mm), which is in clear contradiction with the experimental observations.
source: Mathematical modelling of the chain model-dependent filament elongation dynamics predicted a linear growth up to a very long flagellum (>0.1 mm), which is in clear contradiction with the experimental observations (Appendix 2).
evidence: Mathematical modeling results compared to experimental data

claim: CCCP treatment resulted in impaired filament extension in a dose-dependent manner, which recovered upon removal of the uncoupler.
source: As expected, CCCP treatment resulted in impaired filament extension in a dose-dependent manner, which recovered upon removal of the uncoupler (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental observation from CCCP treatment experiments, supported by Figure 6a

claim: The injection-diffusion model predicts that a decrease in the injection rate Kon results in slow, quasi-linear growth for sufficiently small Kon.
source: The injection-diffusion model predicts that a decrease in the injection rate Kon results in slow, quasi-linear growth for sufficiently small Kon.
evidence: Prediction from the mathematical model

claim: The filament elongation rate for the highest CCCP concentration (~18 nm∙min−1) was virtually independent of the length of the filament as predicted by the model.
source: As shown in Figure 6c, the filament elongation rate for the highest CCCP concentration (~18 nm∙min−1) was virtually independent of the length of the filament as predicted by the model.
evidence: Experimental observation matching model prediction, supported by Figure 6c

claim: Some filaments were unaffected by the CCCP treatment, likely due to the action of multidrug transporters, and displayed kinetics similar to the untreated population.
source: Interestingly, some filaments were unaffected by the CCCP treatment, likely due to the action of multidrug transporters (Lomovskaya and Lewis, 1992), and displayed kinetics similar to the untreated population (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d)
evidence: Experimental observation with inference about mechanism, supported by citation and Figure 6—figure supplement 1d

claim: The rate of flagellum growth, initially ∼1,700 amino acids per second, decreases with length.
source: We report that the rate of flagellum growth, initially ∼1,700 amino acids per second, decreases with length
evidence: Experimental finding reported in the abstract

claim: The previously proposed chain mechanism does not contribute to the filament elongation dynamics.
source: We report that the rate of flagellum growth, initially ∼1,700 amino acids per second, decreases with length and that the previously proposed chain mechanism does not contribute to the filament elongation dynamics.
evidence: Experimental finding reported in the abstract

claim: Inhibition of the proton motive force-dependent export apparatus revealed a major contribution of substrate injection in driving filament elongation.
source: Inhibition of the proton motive force-dependent export apparatus revealed a major contribution of substrate injection in driving filament elongation.
evidence: Experimental finding from CCCP experiments reported in the abstract

claim: A simple, injection-diffusion mechanism controls bacterial flagella growth outside the cell.
source: The combination of experimental and mathematical evidence demonstrates that a simple, injection-diffusion mechanism controls bacterial flagella growth outside the cell.
evidence: Main conclusion combining experimental and mathematical evidence

claim: Bacterial flagella grow through an injection-diffusion mechanism.
source: We propose that bacterial flagella grow through an injection-diffusion mechanism (Figure 6d)
evidence: Main conclusion of the study, supported by Figure 6d

claim: The injection-diffusion mechanism provides a simple explanation why the flagellar filament does not grow infinitely in the absence of any other length-control mechanism.
source: We propose that bacterial flagella grow through an injection-diffusion mechanism (Figure 6d), which provides a simple explanation why the flagellar filament does not grow infinitely in the absence of any other length-control mechanism.
evidence: Inference from the model

claim: Similar biophysical principles are likely conserved for effector protein secretion in the evolutionary related, virulence-associated injectisome.
source: It appears likely that similar biophysical principles are conserved for effector protein secretion in the evolutionary related, virulence-associated injectisome with important implications for the rational design of novel anti-infectives targeted against type III secretion systems.
evidence: Speculation about broader implications

claim: A flagellar filament of 1 µm length is composed of approximately 2130 flagellin subunits.
source: Using β = 0.47 nm (a flagellar filament of 1 µm length is composed of approximately 2130 flagellin subunits [Yonekura et al., 2003])
evidence: Structural parameter from citation

claim: The values for kon decrease by a factor of 8 (10 µM CCCP), 22 (20 µM CCCP), and 38 (30 µM CCCP), compared to the untreated control.
source: The values for kon decrease by a factor of 8 (10 µM CCCP), 22 (20 µM CCCP), and 38 (30 µM CCCP), compared to the untreated control.
evidence: Quantitative result from fitting model to CCCP treatment data
